Six overlapping flat sheets hang in layers, each taller than the fae herself, wavy-hemmed, their faces crowded with six-sided cups — the sealed ones burning swollen gold, the front sheet's lowest hem pooling honey that drops in slow fat beads, one bead still mid-fall and perfectly amber.

A sheet broken clean off, its torn upper edge pouring honey thick and slow, each broken cup catching the light all down the wound, the six-sided faces of the sheets behind showing as pale gold shapes through the pour — one empty cup at the far corner stoppered with pine resin.

Seven sheets layered back behind back, the front crowded with forty or more clinging bodies each no longer than two wax cups across, the rearmost sheets so old they have gone tough dark amber, the newest at the front pale as cream, both colours burning where the light drives through.

A whole sheet's pale sealing skin peeled back in one piece, left hanging by its corner, translucent as new bone with light behind it, every cup beneath brimming and open, honey welling from three broken ones and running down the face of the sheet below in three slow amber ropes.

One sheet held up flat so the light punches straight through — lens-clear molten gold where full honey backs the cups, milky cream where they are dry and open, the six-sided lattice standing hard against the glare, a small acorn cup already wedged beneath the lowest wavy hem to catch what runs.

The front sheet half stripped: its upper cups open, dry and ragged, the wax torn back in pale flakes, while the sealed lower band glows swollen behind skins the colour of new bone — honey welling from two broken cups and threading down across forty or more clinging bodies below.

Five overlapping sheets, the second one beginning to sag in the warmth, its lower hem stretching outward and losing its shape, the six-sided cups along the sag pulling long at their mouths, honey seeping from the distorted ones and running warm and heavy down the face of the sheet beneath.

The oldest two sheets at the back gone dark amber and stiff with age, the three in front pale cream and swollen, the very front one still entirely sealed, every cup shut under its skin of new-bone wax, the whole face glowing even — one cup at its edge already weeping gold.

A sheet with its bottom-left corner bitten away, the break raw and running, the little six-sided cups along the edge standing open and brimming, honey dripping from the torn hem in a short curtain of fat amber beads — a folded-leaf pail wedged into the wavy hem directly below.

Fresh wax built out in pale scallops from one sheet's right edge, each new cup still soft and cup-shaped and barely sealed, the half-finished cups open to the light and glowing faint cream, honey already pooling in the lowest finished ones, pulling the soft hem downward in a slow droop.

Four sheets in layers, the front one's upper third stripped clean — cups open, dry, their wax edges ragged — the sealed middle band burning solid gold behind new-bone skins, and at the very bottom the wavy hem pooling honey so heavy it drops in slow beads, one bead mid-fall.

Two sheets pressed close, the front pale and new, the rear dark and stiff with age, the light splitting between them — cream through the front, deep amber through the back — honey from three broken cups on the front face running down and catching both colours at once as it falls.

A single whole sheet tipped sideways by a grass-cord line tied round its edge, its face of six-sided cups tilting toward the light, the sealed ones going lens-clear gold on their lower halves where honey pools under its own weight, the upper cups pale and dry, one still sealed cup glowing brighter than all the rest.

Six overlapping sheets, the front one covered in sixty or more clinging bodies each no longer than two cups across, the sheets behind showing only as layered pale shapes through the mass, honey welling from one broken cup at chest height and running down across the clinging shapes below.

A sheet sagging soft in the warmth, its lower hem stretching into a long droop, the six-sided cups along the droop distorting at their mouths, honey running from the weakest ones and meeting at the lowest point — a hollow rose-hip, already amber-brimmed, wedged into the hem below it.

Seven sheets hanging in layers, the front entirely sealed, its whole face glowing even behind skins the colour of new bone, not one cup broken — then one corner gives, a single crack running six cups wide, honey welling from all six at once in a slow gold spill down the face.

The front sheet's pale sealing skin peeled halfway back, the freed flap hanging and still translucent enough to show the full cups through it glowing gold, while the uncovered cups brim open, honey running from the lowest ones down across the faces of the sheets below in thin bright ropes.

Three sheets, the rearmost so old it has gone dark amber and stiff, the middle one pale gold, the front one cream-white and new, all three glowing a different depth of gold when the light drives through them — honey pooled in each lower hem, the front hem dropping slow fat beads.

A slab of honeycomb broken off and held up edge-on, the flat sheets of its layers standing edge-on as a stack of thin leaves, each one a thin leaf of wax with six-sided cups on both faces, the sealed cups burning molten gold all through the slab, honey pouring from the broken edge thick and slow in one unbroken run.

Five overlapping sheets, honey welling from four broken cups along the face of the second one, each trickle finding the wavy lower hem of the sheet below, pooling there and dropping — a section of hollow reed, stoppered at one end with resin, propped to catch the steady fall from the lowest hem.

The front sheet half stripped from the top, its upper cups open and pale and dry, the intact lower band still sealed and swollen, glowing gold behind skins of new bone — and across the open dry upper cups, sixty or more clinging bodies each no longer than two cups across.

One sheet with a scalloped fringe of new wax being built out from its bottom edge, each new pale cup soft and open, the finished cups just behind already sealing over, their skins going from clear to new-bone white as the wax sets — one unfinished cup still so soft it holds a bead of honey suspended in its open mouth.

Six sheets in layers, the front one carrying honey pooled deep in its wavy hem, so heavy the hem is pulling the sheet longer than the others, the sealed cups above the pool still burning even gold — a cupped bark scoop, its inner face bright with the honey already in it, tucked into the hem below.

A sheet's face with the pale sealing skins still intact over all its cups, the whole surface glowing new-bone white and even in the light — then the light shifts slightly and the gold inside each cup burns through the skin like a lattice of small amber lanterns set behind frosted wax.

Five overlapping sheets, honey running from a break near the top of the front one, threading down across the six-sided cups below it, following the slight lean of the sheet, gathering at the wavy hem, pooling, then dropping — a large snail shell, its opening tilted upward, already a quarter full of running gold.
